title: Data center site due diligence: feasibility screen first, then a utility-grade power study
description: How data center site due diligence works in two steps: a feasibility screen (power, flood, seismic, wetlands, FAA, zoning) and a utility-grade power study with N-1 tests.
intro: Data center site due diligence answers two questions in order. Is this site worth more money and time? And how much power can it get, by when, and at what cost? Invariant splits the work the same way. Step one is a feasibility screen: from a coordinate and a MW figure we check power at the nearest substations, flood zone, seismic hazard, wetlands, airports, zoning and the parcel, and end in a go or no-go. Step two is a utility-grade power study for the sites that pass: an AC power flow with N-1 contingency tests at each connection option, the upgrades that lift the limit, an indicative cost and an energization date.
takeaways: Screen many sites cheaply, then study the few that survive. Most sites fail on something you can check in a day.
Distance to a line is not capacity. Paces found only about 17% of ERCOT substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom.
A utility load study costs $10,000 to $100,000 or more and needs site control. Run your own study first so you file at the right point with the right MW.
Our MW figures are screening figures built to utility planning methods. The utility’s own study is what makes a number firm.

sections.heading: The two steps and what each one decides

blocks.text: Most site deals die for boring reasons: a floodway across the pad, a county moratorium, a substation that is already spoken for. None of those need a power flow to find. So the first pass is wide and fast, and the expensive work only goes to sites that have earned it.

blocks.text: Who buys this? Developers deciding which options to exercise, investors and lenders underwriting powered land, AI companies and neoclouds choosing between shortlisted sites, landowners who want to know what their land is worth to a data center, and brokers and advisers who want the work done behind their own name.

The screen is a set of kill checks run in a fixed order, cheapest first. The power check comes first because it kills the most sites. A site 20 miles from any 138 kV or higher station rarely makes sense above a few MW, whatever else it has going for it.

blocks.text: Every finding carries its source. Where we cannot settle something from records, the report says so and names the document or call that would settle it.

A utility decides how much load a site can take by running a power flow on its planning model and testing what happens when a line or transformer trips. We run the same kind of study, on a model of the network we rebuild around your site, before you spend a study deposit or post security.

blocks.text: The answer comes out as a MW figure per connection point per study year, the line or transformer that sets each figure, and what it would take to lift it. That is the information you need to pick a point of interconnection, size a first phase and judge a seller’s claims.

sections.heading: Why proximity to a line misleads

blocks.text: The most common mistake in powered land is reading a transmission map as a capacity map. A 345 kV line beside the parcel tells you a tap is physically possible. It says nothing about whether the line, the next substation or the transformers upstream can carry another 200 MW when one element is out of service.
In a 2025 analysis of ERCOT, Paces found only about 17% of substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom.

We see the same pattern in our own studies. In one recent Gulf Coast study, the two nearest 138 kV substations could take only a few MW in the first study year, while a new 345 kV switching station on circuits running past the site could take about 200 MW. Same parcel. Very different answer depending on where you connect.

sections.heading: Where our study sits next to the utility’s

blocks.text: Utilities run their own studies once you apply with site control, and those are the only studies that commit them. AEP Ohio charges $10,000 to $100,000 for a data center study depending on size. Texas set a $100,000 study fee for large loads in ERCOT.

Our study does not replace that step. It makes it count: you file at the connection point most likely to work, at a MW figure the network can carry, with a list of questions that gets real answers in the pre-application meeting. Every report states that its figures are screening figures and that the utility’s study makes them firm.

Equity investors buy this kind of diligence too. Ankura’s case study of a 300 MW brownfield for an institutional investor covered 230 kV line and substation feasibility, ISO timing, zoning, gas supply, cooling water and a risk matrix.

faqs.question: What is data center site due diligence?
faqs.answer: It is the work that tells a buyer whether a site can be built on and powered, by when and at what cost. It covers power and interconnection, flood, seismic and ground conditions, wetlands and species, airspace, zoning and local approval, water, fiber and the parcel. faqs.question: What is the difference between a feasibility study and a power study for a data center?
faqs.answer: A feasibility screen checks whether a site has a fatal flaw and gives a first range of MW at nearby substations. A power study runs an AC power flow with N-1 contingency tests at each connection option and returns MW by year, the binding element, the upgrades needed, an indicative cost and an energization date.

faqs.question: How long does data center site due diligence take?
faqs.answer: Invariant returns a feasibility screen within 24 hours of receiving a coordinate and a MW figure, and a utility-grade power study usually within 48 hours. faqs.question: Can a site be judged by its distance to a transmission line?
faqs.answer: No. Distance shows a connection is physically possible, not that the network can carry the load. Paces found only about 17% of ERCOT substations near suitable land had withdrawal headroom.

blocks.text: The order matters. We run power first, then flood, then the rest, and stop writing when a site fails a hard check. You still get the full record, but the verdict is on page one.

sections.heading: The power check in the screen

blocks.text: We identify the serving utility and balancing area, then every substation and line within reach of the site at a voltage that can carry the load. As a rough guide, 69 kV serves loads up to about 60 MW, 138 kV up to about 200 MW, 230 kV up to about 400 MW and 345 kV up to about 1,000 MW. A radial station fails any load that needs N-1 service.

For each candidate point we estimate headroom from the line and transformer ratings around it, minus the load already announced or filed nearby, for each of the next three study years. The output is a low, mid and high MW figure and the element that sets it.
Hosting capacity maps rarely help here. Nearly all of them cover distribution feeders and generation, not large loads on the transmission system.
Flood comes from FEMA’s National Flood Hazard Layer: we check the zone under the pad, the access road and the substation route, and flag anything in a 1% annual chance zone.

Seismic comes from the USGS National Seismic Hazard Model and the ASCE Hazard Tool, which give the ground motion values a structural engineer will design to. Wetlands come from the National Wetlands Inventory and listed species from IPaC. Airspace comes from the FAA’s notice criteria under Part 77.

Then the local layer: zoning, data center moratoriums and recent votes in the county, parcel ownership and size, water and wastewater, fiber routes and gas for on-site generation. Data Center Watch tracks projects blocked or delayed by local opposition; we check the county against it and against local news.

title: Utility-grade power study for data centers: N-1 power flow before you file with the utility
description: A utility-grade power study for a data center site: AC power flow and N-1 contingency tests at each connection point, MW by year, upgrades, indicative cost and energization date.
intro: A utility-grade power study tells you how many MW a site can take at each possible connection point, in each study year, and what limits it. Invariant rebuilds the transmission network around your site, checks the model against flows the ISO publishes, injects your load and runs AC power flow with N-1 contingency tests in the way a utility planner would under NERC TPL-001. You get MW by connection point and year, the line or transformer that binds, the upgrade that lifts it, an indicative cost and an energization date range. Usually within 48 hours.
takeaways: Built to utility planning methods: seasonal cases, study years, N-0 and N-1, thermal and voltage limits.
Every connection option is tested, including a new switching station on lines that pass the site.
Upgrades come with the MW they unlock, so you can see what a bigger first phase would cost.
It is a screening study. The utility’s own study makes a number firm, and the report says so.

rows: The transmission system around the site rebuilt for each study year, checked against flows the ISO publishes
Summer peak, winter peak and light load, near-term and later study years, with competing loads in and out
Your MW, ramp and power factor at each candidate point of interconnection, including new switching stations on nearby lines
AC power flow at N-0 and N-1 for every element in the study area (NERC TPL-001 P1), plus selected breaker and common-tower events
Thermal limits against normal and emergency ratings, voltage limits, the element that binds first and at what MW
Short circuit level and short circuit ratio at the point of interconnection, with a flag where dynamic studies are likely
The fix for each violation and the MW it unlocks: reconductoring, a second transformer, a new bay, a new line
Indicative cost ranges from unit costs and a dated energization range from the utility process and lead times
Tariff, study fees, security, minimum bills and the questions to bring to the pre-application meeting

blocks.text: The report reads answer first: the MW you can plan on, where, and from when. The method, the cases and the full contingency results follow for your engineers.

We start by building the network: substations, lines, transformers and generation around the site, with the ratings and the planned changes that will be in service by each study year, including generator retirements from EIA-860M and announced large loads nearby.

Then we check the base case. Area totals and flows on major paths must line up with what the ISO reports before any load goes in. A model that cannot reproduce today’s grid cannot tell you about 2029.

Then we add your load at each candidate point and push it up until something breaks. A linear transfer screen ranks the elements most exposed to the new load. A full AC solve at N-0 and N-1, over every element in the study area, finds the MW at which the first thermal or voltage limit is crossed. NERC calls the single-element outages P1 events; we add selected P2, P4, P5 and P7 events for the elements that bind.

For each violation we try the fix a utility would likely propose, re-solve, and record the MW it unlocks. That gives three numbers per connection point: MW with no upgrades, MW with only the facilities to connect you, and MW with network upgrades.

sections.heading: Why grid strength now matters for AI loads

blocks.text: Large AI training loads swing fast and ride through faults differently from older loads. NERC issued a Level 2 alert on large loads asking planners how they model and study them, and ERCOT has published work on modeling large data center loads.

We report short circuit level and short circuit ratio at each connection point and flag where a utility is likely to ask for dynamic or electromagnetic transient studies. That flag can move a schedule by months.

Indicative costs come from unit cost tables for lines and substation work. MISO’s MTEP24 guide, for example, gives about $1.9 to $2.3 million a mile for a new single-circuit 138 kV line and $3.2 to $4.1 million a mile at 345 kV, and about $15.8 million for a new four-position 345 kV ring bus. We carry ranges, never point figures.

The date range adds up the utility’s intake and study clock, the agreement, and the longer of the network build or long-lead equipment such as large transformers. In Texas that clock now runs through ERCOT’s batch process for large loads.

sections.heading: How it relates to the utility’s study

blocks.text: Our study is not the utility’s case and does not commit the utility to anything. The utility’s study, run on its own planning model once you apply with site control, is what makes a number firm. What ours does is tell you where to apply, how much to ask for, which upgrades to expect and which questions to bring to the pre-application meeting.

That matters because applying is expensive. AEP Ohio charges up to $100,000 for a data center study; Texas charges $100,000 for large loads in ERCOT, with security on top. A wrong point of interconnection or an oversized request costs months.

title: Power flow study for a data center: what it tests and how to read the results
description: What a power flow (load flow) study is for a data center interconnection, what it tests, what inputs it needs, and how to read the MW, the binding element and the upgrades.
intro: A power flow study, also called a load flow study, solves the voltages and the flow on every line and transformer in a network for a given pattern of load and generation. For a data center it answers one question: if this much load connects here, does any element go over its rating or any voltage go out of range, with everything in service and with any one element out? The MW at which the first limit is crossed is the site’s headroom at that point.
takeaways: A power flow is a snapshot. Planners run several: summer and winter peak, light load, and more than one study year.
The answer depends on the connection point. Two substations a mile apart can differ by hundreds of MW.
The binding element is often not the nearest one. It can be a transformer two stations away.
Utilities study in tools such as Siemens PSS/E on their planning cases, which are protected as CEII.

blocks.text: Give the solver the network (buses, lines, transformers, their impedances and ratings), the generation dispatch and the loads, and it finds a consistent set of voltages and flows. An AC power flow includes reactive power and voltage. A DC power flow is a fast linear version used to screen many cases.

Utility planners run these on base cases built for each season and study year. The cases are protected as critical energy infrastructure information, so access needs an agreement with the ISO or FERC.

sections.heading: Inputs for a data center study

items: The site location and each candidate point of interconnection, including a new switching station on a passing line.
The load in MW for each phase and year, and its power factor.
The study years that match your ramp.
Planned grid changes in service by each year: new lines, upgrades, generator retirements.
Other large loads likely to connect nearby, because they use the same headroom.

rows: 345/138 kV transformer at a neighbouring station, N-1
138 kV line out of B, N-1
New switching station on line C, 345 kV
Voltage at the new bus after loss of the parallel circuit

blocks.text: The table above shows the format, not a real site. Read it by connection point and year. A high number in year three with a low number in year one tells you to phase the load or wait for a planned upgrade.

sections.heading: Common mistakes in reading a power flow

blocks.text: Taking one season as the answer is the usual one. A site can be fine at summer peak and fail at light load when local generation is off. Another: ignoring the load queue. If two other data centers are filing at the same substation, the headroom you found is shared.
And a study that does not name its binding element is not worth much. You need the element to judge the fix and to ask the utility the right question.

title: How N-1 contingency analysis tests a data center’s power headroom
description: A worked 60 MW example shows how a connection can pass with both lines in service and exceed its thermal limit after a single outage.
intro: An N-1 contingency analysis tests how the grid responds when one element goes out of service. For a proposed data center, a load that fits with both lines in service can overload the remaining line after an outage. The two-line example below starts with 120 MW of existing demand. A 60 MW addition passes the normal case, but the worst outage leaves room for only 35 MW of additional load.
takeaways: Ask for the binding outage and the equipment or study criterion that limits the load.
Compare results at the same connection point, study year, and facility load in MW.
Check the utility’s service terms for milestones, required upgrades, and any curtailment conditions.

blocks.text: In NERC’s transmission planning standard, P0 is the normal system condition. P1 includes specified single events, such as the loss of a transmission circuit, a transformer, a generator, or a shunt device. Other categories cover events such as bus faults and overlapping outages. The criteria and events for a particular connection depend on the utility, the system, and the study scope.

For each applicable case, ask which equipment ratings and voltage limits the study uses and what system changes or operating actions it assumes. An outage can shift flow onto equipment several stations away. A standby generator at the facility changes the load seen by the grid only if its operation is represented in the case.

sections.heading: A 60 MW request that passes until a line is out

blocks.text: Take a simplified, lossless example with two parallel lines supplying 120 MW of existing demand. With both lines in service, assume Line A carries 60% of the load and Line B carries 40%. Use thermal limits of 170 MW and 155 MW respectively. When one line is out, assume the remaining line must carry all of the demand. Add a 60 MW facility at the same load point.

rows: Line B exceeds its limit by 25 MW
Line A exceeds its limit by 10 MW

blocks.text: Under these assumptions, Line B sets the limit when Line A is out. Subtract the existing 120 MW from its 155 MW limit and the modeled margin is 35 MW. The normal operating condition alone would miss that constraint. This example isolates one thermal limit. A real study can also find voltage or stability constraints, use different allowable ratings during outages, and test whether network changes resolve the problem.

sections.heading: What to ask when you read the result

blocks.text: Get the point of interconnection, study year, starting demand, and case assumptions with each headroom figure. Ask whether the study represents nearby committed load and planned upgrades. A load that meets the thermal limits can still require voltage or stability analysis. ERCOT’s large-load stability guidance, for example, calls for peak and off-peak cases, relevant contingencies, and nearby loads with signed interconnection agreements.

If the first phase misses its target, ask the utility what would change the result. The options could include a different connection point, a smaller initial phase, an upgrade, or an operating limit. Confirm which options the utility will accept, what each phase can draw at the meter, and what has to happen before service can begin.

faqs.question: What does N-1 mean in power systems?
faqs.answer: It means evaluating the system with one element out of service. Specify which outage, which equipment and limits are monitored, and which operating actions are allowed.

faqs.question: What is the difference between N-1 and N-1-1?
faqs.answer: N-1 applies a single outage. In N-1-1, a second outage follows the first, with time for specified system adjustments in between. NERC’s P6 category covers specified overlapping single events.

faqs.question: Does 35 MW of modeled headroom mean the site can get 35 MW?
faqs.answer: The 35 MW applies only to the example’s thermal limits and operating assumptions. For a real connection, the utility can identify the required studies and document the available service, upgrades, and conditions.

title: How to check if a substation has capacity for a data center
description: How to check substation capacity for a data center: what you can learn from records, why hosting capacity maps miss large loads, and when you need a power flow study.
intro: You cannot read a substation’s spare capacity off a map, and most utilities will not tell you without a paid, site-controlled study. What you can do before that is narrow it down: find the stations within reach, check their voltage and how many lines feed them, estimate headroom from the ratings around them, subtract the load already filed nearby, and then run a power flow with N-1 tests on the ones that survive. That is what Invariant’s two-step due diligence does.
takeaways: Voltage sets the ceiling. As a rough guide, 138 kV supports up to about 200 MW and 345 kV up to about 1,000 MW.
A station fed by one line is radial and fails any load that needs firm service.
Hosting capacity maps are almost all about distribution and generation, not large loads.
The load already queued at a station is mostly not disclosed, so it has to be estimated from filings.

sections.heading: What you can find without the utility

items: The serving utility for the parcel, from EIA-861 service territory data.
Substations and lines within reach, their voltage and how many lines connect at each.
Generator retirements and additions nearby from EIA-860M, which free up or take up capacity.
Announced data centers, industrial loads and rezoning filings near each station.
The utility’s large-load tariff, study fees and minimum bills.

sections.heading: Why hosting capacity maps do not answer it

blocks.text: Many utilities publish hosting capacity maps, and the Department of Energy keeps an atlas of them. Nearly all show how much generation or load a distribution feeder can take. A 50 MW or 500 MW data center connects to the transmission system, which those maps do not cover.

sections.heading: What the utility will and will not say

blocks.text: Utilities usually confirm territory and will talk through a project informally. Dominion, for example, runs a data center request process with an early feasibility look before paid engineering. Specific spare capacity at a named station almost always waits for a paid, site-controlled study.

That is why a pre-study matters. If you walk into the pre-application meeting knowing which station binds and why, you can ask a question the utility can answer: is the spare transformer capacity at station X already committed?

sections.heading: When to run a full study

blocks.text: Run a power flow with contingency tests once a site passes the screen and you are about to spend real money on it: an option payment, a study deposit, or an LOI. Paces found only about 17% of ERCOT substations near suitable land had withdrawal headroom, so the screen will remove most candidates before then.

faqs.answer: Narrow it down from records (voltage, line count, ratings, nearby loads and retirements), then run a power flow with N-1 tests. The utility confirms capacity only through its own study after you apply with site control.

faqs.question: Do utilities publish substation capacity?
faqs.answer: Mostly no, for large loads. Hosting capacity maps cover distribution feeders and generation. Transmission planning cases are protected as CEII.

faqs.question: What voltage does a data center need?
faqs.answer: As a rough guide, 69 kV serves up to about 60 MW, 138 kV up to about 200 MW, 230 kV up to about 400 MW and 345 kV or higher beyond that. The real limit depends on the network around the station.

faqs.question: Can Invariant check a substation for me?

title: Data Center Utility Load Study Cost, Fees and Timeline
description: Compare AEP Ohio load study fees, ERCOT study charges and financial security, and Dominion’s engineering process. See the cost assumptions for a 100 MW request.
intro: AEP Ohio lists study fees of $10,000 to $100,000 based on the MW requested. Texas sets a $100,000 study fee for covered large-load requests in ERCOT. A 100 MW new request under the standard Texas process also carries $5 million in baseline financial security at the intermediate agreement. Track each payment, the study date and the earliest utility service date separately before committing to land.
takeaways: AEP Ohio lists $50,000 at exactly 50 MW and $100,000 at exactly 100 MW. Get written confirmation at the tariff’s 25 MW boundary.
AEP Ohio describes reasonable-effort study periods of 45 or 60 days, depending on whether regional transmission upgrades are needed.
For an ordinary covered Texas request, $50,000 per requested MW sets the baseline intermediate financial security. Construction contributions and later security have separate terms.
Get the study scope, conditions, payment triggers and date of each service milestone for the specific point of connection.

sections.heading: How much does a utility load study cost?

blocks.text: Start with the utility that will serve the site and the facility demand at the meter. The Ohio bands below come from AEP Ohio’s application instructions. The Texas figure comes from the adopted rule effective October 8, 2026. Dominion describes a project-specific engineering process.

rows: Confirm treatment in writing at exactly 25 MW.
Use the MW requested on the application.
Confirm the tranche and submission cutoff with Ohio Power.
Due by execution of the intermediate agreement. Additional ERCOT study fees may apply under its protocols.
Ask for the engineering agreement, its scope and the expected date for a service plan.

blocks.text: AEP Ohio’s intake page describes the formal process at 25 MW and above, while the November 2026 tariff defines a data center under Schedule DCT using demand greater than 25 MW. The published fee table also starts above 25 MW. Ask Ohio Power for the classification and fee when the planned request lands exactly on that boundary.

sections.heading: What does a 100 MW request commit?

blocks.text: This example uses a new 100 MW facility request. Get the utility’s written amounts and due dates for your project. Keep the study invoice, financial security, construction contributions and ongoing minimum charges on separate lines.

rows: Check the LOA, collateral, and monthly demand provisions. At 100 MW post-ramp contract capacity, the tariff-based minimum is 82.5 MW before comparison with the prior-demand rule.
$100,000 study fee plus $5 million in baseline financial security at the intermediate agreement.
Ask what qualifies as security and whether equipment, construction contributions, additional fees or allocated upgrades raise later obligations.

blocks.text: Texas §25.194(d)(2) sets the $5 million baseline as 100 MW × $50,000 per requested MW. Certain early equipment and service commitments can require additional security or direct payment. At the standard large-load interconnection agreement stage, the rule sets security at the greater of $50,000 per contracted MW and the allocated system-upgrade cost, with possible other obligations under the applicable terms.

Under AEP Ohio Schedule DCT, 100 MW of post-ramp contract capacity gives a tariff minimum of 57.5 MW plus 25 MW, or 82.5 MW, subject to the stated cap on that part of the formula. The other test uses 85% of the highest previously established monthly billing demand in the past 11 months. The higher test sets the floor after ramp. During ramp, the tariff instead applies 85% of the load-ramp contract capacity. Keep these demand quantities separate from the utility’s dollar rates.

blocks.label: Download the study fee and security evidence

sections.heading: How long does a utility load study take?

blocks.text: Ohio Power says it will make reasonable efforts to complete a paid study within 60 days when regional transmission upgrades are needed and 45 days otherwise. The program can group projects by tranche or upgrade. Ask when your case enters study and what triggers the estimated completion date.

In ERCOT, ask the serving utility which study process applies to your request and what the queue and engineering milestones mean for each phase. In Dominion Virginia, the published process starts with feasibility, then identifies the scope of the engineering and construction agreements. Confirm when the utility can provide initial load, when it expects permanent service and which facilities control each date.

items.label: Compare the utility documents that support a delivery date

sections.heading: What to verify before paying for a study

blocks.text: Bring the parcel, proposed meter location, initial and final facility MW, phased dates, expected reliability, and any on-site generation. Ask which alternate connection points or ramp profiles it will accept. Record what the study will deliver and which utility approval comes next.

Ohio Power lists an executed option, lease or ownership as ways to establish site control for its load study request. Texas §25.194 lists qualifying property interests and documentation for the intermediate agreement. Review the specific evidence your utility will accept before starting a land option or utility filing.

faqs.question: How much does a data center load study cost?
faqs.answer: Ohio Power lists $10,000 above 25 MW and below 50 MW, $50,000 from 50 MW to below 100 MW, and $100,000 starting at 100 MW. The adopted Texas rule sets a $100,000 fee for covered requests, with financial security calculated separately.

faqs.question: How much financial security does a 100 MW Texas request require?
faqs.answer: For an ordinary covered new ERCOT request, the baseline intermediate security is $50,000 per requested MW, or $5 million for 100 MW. Equipment and upgrade obligations can change the amount required at later steps.

faqs.question: How long does a utility load study take?
faqs.answer: Ohio Power describes reasonable-effort periods of 45 days without regional transmission upgrades and 60 days when they are required. Confirm the start milestone, applicable batch, and the separate utility service date for the site.

faqs.question: Do I need site control for a load study?
faqs.answer: Ohio Power requires control of the site for its formal load study and lists ownership, a lease or an option. Covered Texas projects need acceptable site-control evidence for the intermediate agreement. Ask the serving utility which evidence applies to your filing.

title: Distance to substation and transmission for a data center site: what it costs and what it doesn’t tell you
description: How distance to a substation or transmission line affects a data center site: cost per mile by voltage, switching station costs, right-of-way time, and why distance is not capacity.
intro: Distance to the nearest substation or transmission line is the first number everyone asks about a data center site, and it matters for cost and time. A new 345 kV line costs about $3.2 to $4.1 million a mile in MISO’s cost guide, and long lines can take years to permit. But distance is not capacity. A line beside the parcel needs a new switching station to tap, and the network behind it still has to carry the load with one element out.
takeaways: Every mile adds cost and right-of-way risk. Short taps take about two years at best; long new lines take far longer.
Tapping a passing line means building a switching station, about $15.8 million for a four-position 345 kV ring bus in MISO’s guide.
Screen on substations and their networks, not on lines alone.
The best site is often the one a bit further away from a stronger station.

rows: New single circuit line, $ million per mile
New double circuit line, $ million per mile
New four-position ring bus substation, $ million

blocks.text: Costs vary by region and terrain, and they escalate each year. We carry them as ranges in every study.

Straight-line distance understates a real route. We multiply by about 1.3 to allow for roads, parcels and terrain, and check the route for floodplain, wetlands and crossings. We measure to substations at a voltage that can carry the load, not to the nearest line on a map.
In a 2025 analysis of ERCOT, Paces found only about 17% of substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom. A 345 kV line next to a parcel is the start of the question.
That is why step one of our due diligence screens on stations and their headroom, and step two runs a power flow with N-1 on each connection option.

faqs.question: How close does a data center need to be to a substation?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number, but every mile of new line adds roughly $2 to $5 million depending on voltage, plus right-of-way time. Many large sites sit within a few miles of a 230 kV or 345 kV station.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to build a transmission line to a data center?
faqs.answer: MISO’s MTEP24 guide gives about $1.9 to $2.3 million a mile for a new single-circuit 138 kV line and $3.2 to $4.1 million a mile at 345 kV, before substation work.

faqs.question: Is a site next to a transmission line a powered site?
faqs.answer: No. It needs a switching station to tap the line, and the network behind it must carry the load under N-1. Only a study shows whether it can.

faqs.question: Can Invariant tell me the distance and cost for my site?
faqs.answer: Yes. The feasibility screen gives distances to each candidate station and line; the power study adds cost and date ranges for each connection option.

title: Check FEMA flood zones by address for data centers
description: Check FEMA flood zones at three data center addresses in Clifton, Northlake and Atlanta. See where the address point and tax parcel match and how to verify the site.
intro: Start a data center flood check with FEMA’s map and confirm where the address point lands. At 55 Marietta Street NW in Atlanta, the city’s address point and the full mapped tax parcel fall in unshaded Zone X. At 501 Northwest Avenue in Northlake, the address point also falls in Zone X, but the nearby county parcels use other street numbers. Check the parcel, building, electrical yard and access road separately before making a site decision.
takeaways: An address-range match can land beside the property. At 100 Delawanna Avenue, it was about two metres outside the tax lot.
Keep the FEMA zone subtype, map panel, effective date and any applicable map revisions with the result.
Check the building, electrical yard and access route separately. Each can intersect a different hazard area.
Use the local floodplain administrator and a qualified engineer to resolve boundary, elevation and floodway questions before design or acquisition.

sections.heading: FEMA flood zones for three data center addresses

blocks.text: We checked FEMA’s effective National Flood Hazard Layer on November 24, 2026. The Clifton and Northlake checks use Census street-range points. For Atlanta, we matched the city’s address records to the Fulton County tax parcel and checked both the point and the entire parcel.

columns: FEMA result at the address point
rows: Zone X, area of minimal flood hazard. The matched point is about 2 m outside lot 1602_61.03_27.
The full mapped tax lot is also unshaded Zone X. It has 0% overlap with the mapped Special Flood Hazard Area. Passaic County FIRM panels 34031C0259G and 34031C0278G took effect April 17, 2020.
Zone X, area of minimal flood hazard at the Census address-range point. The download includes both FEMA map panel records returned at that point.
Point check only. Cook County returned nearby parcels addressed as 505 and 525 Northwest Avenue. Ask for the parcel ID and site plan for 501 before screening the property.
Zone X, area of minimal flood hazard at the city’s address point. The point is inside Fulton County parcel 14 007800110419.
The full mapped parcel is also unshaded Zone X, with 0% overlap with the mapped Special Flood Hazard Area. FEMA panel 13121C0244F took effect September 18, 2013.

blocks.text: The FEMA point results had no published static base flood elevation. These checks record what the effective map shows at the screened locations. Building elevations, local stormwater and routes into each facility require separate checks.

blocks.label: Download the FEMA point and parcel checks

sections.heading: How to look up a flood zone by address

blocks.text: Enter the complete address, city and ZIP in FEMA’s Flood Map Service Center. Open the effective map and record the zone, subtype, panel ID and effective date. Check for a Letter of Map Amendment or Revision that applies to the structure or parcel.

Identify the tax parcel using the assessor’s address and parcel ID. Compare the returned address point with the parcel and building geometry. If the address lands on a road or outside the lot, use a verified building or proposed pad location for the point check.

For a portfolio or API workflow, Earth can return a mapped point result and calculate the share of a matched parcel in the Special Flood Hazard Area. Keep both geographies in the result and use the downloadable cases to reproduce the source checks.

For a dry building pad with vulnerable access, check route elevations and low points between the site and the public network. For waterfront sites, review storm surge and future water levels alongside the effective map. Inland, review local drainage and soils where stormwater collects.

sections.heading: FEMA flood zones in plain terms

rows: Special Flood Hazard Area. These zones describe different 1% annual-chance flooding conditions.
Check the mapped elevation or depth, datum and applicable local floodplain requirements.
Coastal Special Flood Hazard Area with wave action.
Check wave exposure, elevation and local coastal standards.
May show 0.2% annual-chance flood hazard, shallow 1% annual-chance flooding or other conditions identified by the map legend.
Read the exact subtype and panel legend. Check drainage and critical equipment elevations.
X, area of minimal flood hazard
Unshaded Zone X on the effective map.
Check local stormwater maps, observed flood history and access.
Find additional local or engineering evidence before grading the location.

blocks.text: The 1% annual chance is the probability in each year. With independent years and constant flood odds, the chance of at least one event over 30 years is about 26%. A FEMA zone describes mapped conditions for the relevant flood study. Check site-specific grading and changing drainage conditions separately.

sections.heading: What to check before acquiring the site

blocks.text: Overlay the planned data halls, switchgear, generators, substation, and the routes needed for service, fuel deliveries and emergency access. Compare site elevations with a published base flood elevation in the same vertical datum. Where FEMA has no static base flood elevation, record it as unavailable and get the applicable study or engineering survey.

Check the regulatory floodway separately from the flood zone. Under 44 CFR 60.3(d)(3), communities generally prohibit encroachments in an adopted regulatory floodway unless technical analyses demonstrate no increase in flood levels for the base flood. The regulation describes a separate conditional map-revision process for certain proposals that would increase flood levels. Confirm local requirements and the project’s path with the floodplain administrator.

title: Data center seismic risk screening: USGS hazard maps, ASCE 7 values and faults
description: How to screen a data center site for seismic risk: the USGS National Seismic Hazard Model, ASCE 7 seismic design category, site soils and mapped faults.
intro: Screen a data center site for seismic risk with three sources: the USGS National Seismic Hazard Model for how hard the ground is likely to shake, the ASCE Hazard Tool for the design values a structural engineer will use, and USGS fault maps for any active fault near the pad. The result is a seismic design category from A (low) to F (highest) that drives structural cost, equipment anchoring and sometimes insurance. USGS’s 2023 model found nearly three quarters of the US could see damaging shaking.
takeaways: Seismic design category depends on both the hazard and the soil. Soft soils amplify shaking.
Higher categories add structural steel, bracing and anchoring for racks, chillers and generators.
Mapped active faults through the pad are usually a kill.
Liquefaction-prone soils near rivers and coasts deserve a geotechnical look early.

blocks.text: The USGS National Seismic Hazard Model estimates ground shaking across the US. Its 2023 update found nearly 75% of the country could experience damaging shaking.

The ASCE Hazard Tool turns a coordinate into the ASCE 7 design values (spectral accelerations) along with wind, snow, ice and flood loads. USGS keeps a database of faults active in the Quaternary period.

columns: What it usually means for a data center
rows: High; added structural cost, anchored and braced equipment, closer review
Very high or near an active fault; specialist design, often avoided

blocks.text: The category also depends on the building’s risk category and the site soil class, which a geotechnical report confirms. The screen gives the expected range; the geotech settles it.

sections.heading: How we use it in the screen

blocks.text: We pull the hazard values and fault distances for the coordinate, check soils for liquefaction risk, and flag the expected design category. In most of the central US this is a quick pass. In the West, around New Madrid and in parts of the Southeast it can move cost and schedule.

title: Data center environmental screening: wetlands, endangered species and Phase I ESA
description: How to screen a data center site for wetlands, listed species and contamination before you buy: National Wetlands Inventory, IPaC, EPA cleanup records and the Phase I ESA.
intro: An environmental screen for a data center site checks three things before you buy: wetlands and streams that would need a Clean Water Act permit to fill, federally listed species that could need consultation or seasonal limits, and contamination that could make you liable for cleanup. Start with the National Wetlands Inventory, the Fish and Wildlife Service’s IPaC tool and EPA cleanup records. Then commission a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment under ASTM E1527-21 before closing.
takeaways: National Wetlands Inventory maps are a screen, not a jurisdictional determination. The Army Corps decides that.
IPaC lists species that may be present; a federal nexus such as a Corps permit triggers consultation.
A Phase I ESA to ASTM E1527-21 supports the All Appropriate Inquiries defence against cleanup liability.
Brownfields and retired plants carry the most contamination risk and often the best power.

blocks.text: The Wetlands Mapper shows mapped wetlands and deepwater habitat. On a large campus even a few acres of wetland in the wrong place can force a redesign or a permit that takes months. We overlay it with the pad, the substation and the line route.
Hydric soils from the Web Soil Survey often flag unmapped wetlands, so we check those too.

IPaC returns the federally listed species and critical habitat that may be near a site. It is common for a site to list a bat or a bird species; what matters is whether there is habitat on the parcel and whether the project has a federal permit that triggers consultation. Tree clearing windows are the usual practical result.

sections.heading: Contamination and the Phase I ESA

blocks.text: EPA’s Cleanups in My Community shows Superfund, brownfield and RCRA sites nearby. Retired plants and industrial sites often have coal ash, fuel or solvent history.

Before closing, a Phase I ESA to ASTM E1527-21 is the standard way to meet EPA’s All Appropriate Inquiries rule and protect a buyer from cleanup liability. Parts of it must be done within 180 days of acquisition.

title: FAA height limits near airports: what a data center site needs to check
description: FAA Part 77 for data center sites: when notice is required for buildings, stacks and cranes near airports, the 200 ft and 100:1 tests, and how to check a site.
intro: A data center near an airport may need to file FAA Form 7460-1 before construction. Under 14 CFR Part 77, notice is required for any structure over 200 feet above ground, and for lower structures that would break an imaginary slope from a nearby public-use airport, for example 100 to 1 for 20,000 feet from a runway longer than 3,200 feet. Cranes count. Generator stacks and cooling equipment can count. The FAA’s Notice Criteria Tool tells you from a coordinate and a height.
takeaways: Most data center buildings are well under 200 feet, so the slope tests near airports are what usually apply.
Construction cranes often need their own filing.
File at least 45 days before construction; a determination of hazard can stop or change the design.
Heliports and private airstrips can matter too.

rows: Public-use airports with a runway over 3,200 ft

blocks.text: If a test is met, notice goes to the FAA on Form 7460-1 at least 45 days before construction starts. The FAA then issues a determination of no hazard, sometimes with marking and lighting conditions.
Enter the coordinate, ground elevation and the tallest point (roof, stack, crane) into the FAA’s Notice Criteria Tool. It returns whether notice is required.
In our feasibility screen we list airports and heliports nearby, run the tool at a typical building and crane height for the campus size, and flag any site where height will shape the design.

faqs.question: Does a data center need FAA approval?
faqs.answer: Only if it meets a Part 77 notice test: over 200 feet above ground, or breaking an airport slope surface. Then it files Form 7460-1 and needs a determination of no hazard.

faqs.question: Do construction cranes need FAA notice?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the crane meets a Part 77 notice test. Cranes are often taller than the finished building.

faqs.question: How far from an airport does Part 77 apply?
faqs.answer: Up to 20,000 feet from a runway longer than 3,200 feet at a public-use airport, on a 100 to 1 slope, plus the 200 foot test anywhere.

faqs.question: Is airspace part of Invariant’s screen?
faqs.answer: Yes, alongside power, flood, seismic, wetlands, zoning and the parcel.

title: Power due diligence for data center investors and lenders: what to ask before you underwrite
description: Data center power due diligence for investors and lenders: which utility documents count, what a power study should show, and the red flags in a powered land deal.
intro: For an investor or lender, power due diligence on a data center site comes down to one question: what document stands behind the MW figure in the model, and what would it take to make it firm? A seller’s will-serve letter is a lead. A utility load study for the marketed load at a named point is the first thing worth underwriting. Between the two, an independent power study tells you whether the number is plausible, which upgrades it assumes, and what date is realistic.
takeaways: Underwrite the document, not the headline MW.
Ask which element limits the MW and which upgrades the date assumes.
Model the minimum bill and term in the service agreement, not just the energy price.
Check the county for moratoriums and recent votes before you fund an option.

items: Which utility document supports the MW figure: indication, will-serve, load study, construction agreement or service agreement?
At which point of interconnection, at what voltage, and from which year?
Which upgrades does the date depend on, and who pays for them?
Is security posted, and in whose name?
What are the minimum bill and the term?
Are other large loads filing at the same station?

blocks.text: Our guide to the five rungs of power evidence explains how much each document is worth.

sections.heading: What an independent power study adds

blocks.text: A seller’s study, if there is one, was run for the seller. An independent study tests every connection option, shows the MW by year with and without upgrades, and names the binding element. Where it agrees with the seller, you underwrite with more confidence. Where it does not, you know which question to ask.
Equity buyers already commission this. Ankura’s 300 MW brownfield case for an institutional investor covered line and substation feasibility, ISO timing, zoning, gas, water and a risk matrix.

items: A MW figure with no named point of interconnection.
A date that ignores a planned upgrade or a batch study cycle.
Proximity to a line offered as proof of power.
A county with a moratorium or a recent failed rezoning.
No mention of a minimum bill.

faqs.question: What power documents should a lender require for a data center site?
faqs.answer: At minimum a utility load study for the marketed load at a named point, and ideally a signed construction agreement with security or an electric service agreement. A will-serve letter alone does not reserve capacity.

faqs.question: Should an investor commission an independent power study?
faqs.answer: Yes, before funding an option or LOI. It shows whether the seller’s MW is plausible, which upgrades it depends on, and what date is realistic. Invariant usually returns one within 48 hours.

faqs.question: What is a minimum bill in a data center service agreement?
faqs.answer: The amount owed each month regardless of use, tied to contract demand. Berkeley Lab and Brattle found a median of 80% across new large-load tariffs.

faqs.question: Can Invariant review a seller’s power claims?
faqs.answer: Yes. Send the site and the seller’s documents; we screen it in 24 hours and run a full power study if it passes.

title: Selling land to a data center developer? Get a power study first
description: For landowners and brokers: why a power study changes what data center developers pay for land, what it should show, and how to get one before you market the site.
intro: Data center developers buy power, not acres. Land near a substation with a documented path to tens or hundreds of MW sells at a very different price from the same land with no power answer, and developers will discount for every unknown. A power study before you market the site tells you, and buyers, how many MW the site can likely take, where, and by when. It also tells you early if the answer is no, before you spend months with brokers.
takeaways: A buyer’s first question is how many MW and by when. Have the answer.
Our study is a screening study; the utility’s own study comes later, usually funded by the buyer.
A study that names the connection point and the binding element is far more credible than a map.
Brokers can run studies on their listings and present them under their own name.

blocks.text: Developers screen hundreds of sites and drop any without a credible power path. Paces found only about 17% of ERCOT substations near suitable land had withdrawal headroom, so buyers have learned not to trust proximity.
A site with a study showing, say, 150 MW at a named 345 kV station from a given year moves to the top of the pile. One without goes to the bottom, whatever the acreage.

items: The serving utility and ISO.
Each realistic connection point, its voltage and distance.
MW by year at each point, with and without upgrades.
The element that limits each figure and the likely fix.
An indicative cost and date range.
Flood, wetlands, zoning and other site checks a buyer will run anyway.

blocks.text: Send Invariant the parcel or a coordinate. We screen it within 24 hours and tell you whether a full power study is worth doing. If it is, the full study usually follows within 48 hours, in editable form so you or your broker can use it in marketing.
If you would rather sell to a buyer we know, we also keep a catalogue of powered sites and work with developers looking for them.

faqs.question: Does a power study increase land value for a data center sale?
faqs.answer: It removes the biggest unknown a buyer prices in. Sites with a credible, documented power path are the ones developers shortlist.

faqs.question: Who pays for the utility’s load study when selling land?
faqs.answer: Usually the buyer, after taking site control, because utilities need site control and a defined load. A pre-study by the seller shows the site is worth that step.

faqs.question: Can a broker get a power study on a listing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Invariant runs studies for brokers and advisers and can deliver them under the broker’s name.
